children: By Konrad Putzier

The dramatic stock-market gyrations and Nvidia boardroom chaos of the last two weeks has everyone from Silicon Valley to the White House asking: What would happen to the U.S. economy if the AI boom goes bust?

The answer is that the U.S. economy would take a painful hit, but the magnitude of the fallout remains a live debate among economists, business and financial leaders. Even if the artificial-intelligence market avoids a crash and merely deflates, many believe a significant contraction in AI investment could cripple economic growth.

Over the past two years, the U.S. has become addicted to AI spending. Surging tech stocks and the massive data-center build-out have kept growth humming. Not since the railway boom of the late 19th century has the build-out of a single brand-new industry made up such a large share of gross domestic product. AI investment accounted for a staggering 25% of economic growth in the last year, according to one estimate by Barclays.
Trillion-dollar stock-market swings, rising borrowing for data centers and calls for restrictions on their construction are raising fears that America's biggest growth engine might start to sputter.

Economists disagree over how bad an AI recession might get. Some worry its effects could be worse than those from the dot-com crash of the early 2000s, which led to a recession. Others are more optimistic.
Here's how economists think an AI bust might ripple through the economy:
The wealth effect

Stocks are up around 20% since the start of 2025, mostly because of the AI trade. AI-related stocks have surged ahead of the overall market and this year have accounted for close to half of the S&P 500. "That's a big tailwind for the economy," said Jonathan Millar, senior U.S. economist at Barclays.

The bull market has propped up consumer spending — the main driver of the U.S. economy — because households tend to spend more as their wealth rises. Consumer spending grew at a strong 3.8% in the third quarter, helping push GDP growth to 3.4%. Take that away, and the economic picture darkens.

The last time a stock-market crash triggered a U.S. recession was the dot-com bust. Back then, the S&P 500 fell by around half and the Nasdaq index dropped by close to 80%. But the economic downturn was relatively short-lived, partly because unemployment surged less than during other recessions. Economists say that large drops in stocks, absent other economic pressures, often can lead to only relatively small drops in consumer spending.

An AI bust, potentially caused by disappointing chatbot profits or overbuilding of data centers, might be more painful. Stocks now make up a larger share of household net worth — 35% compared with 26% at the peak of the dot-com bubble.

The top 1% wealthiest households held more than half of all stocks and mutual fund shares owned by individuals as of the second quarter, according to Federal Reserve data, and these rich Americans have also been driving consumer spending. Risky strategies like borrowing against shares are common. If markets tumble, millions of Americans will likely feel the pain and tighten their wallets, which in theory would slow the economy.
Data-center spending

Falling stock prices aren't the only danger. Spending on data-center construction and other AI investment is set to total a far greater share of GDP this year than did the investments in internet infrastructure in the late 1990s and early 2000s. And spending is on track to rise considerably in future years.

Investment in data centers has boosted economic growth, creating jobs in construction and at manufacturers that supply components to the build-out. Companies like Caterpillar, which makes generators, turbine maker GE Vernova and electrical equipment company Eaton have reported surging revenues tied to the data-center boom.
"We love data centers," Dave Regnery, the chief executive of HVAC manufacturer Trane Technologies, said during a recent earnings call.

A flood of Democrats were elected to Congress earlier this month, partly on pledges to rein in the data-center build-out. If they make good on these promises or if investors sour on the technology's potential profits and hyperscalers suddenly pull back on building new data centers, the U.S. economy would lose a key engine.

Still, the impact might be less severe than many fear. Most data-center spending is on imported chips, which add little to domestic GDP. Account for that and data-center construction added around 0.5 percentage point to GDP growth over the past year, estimates Barclays' Millar. If data-center construction went to zero, that could cause a recession in chip-making powerhouse Taiwan — but not necessarily in the U.S.
Borrowing risks

How bad an AI downturn gets could depend on the financial sector. The housing bust turned into the worst recession in more than 70 years largely because trouble spread to financial institutions, which pulled back on lending, choking off the supply of credit that keeps the economy going. Some economists are starting to see parallels between the mid-2000s subprime-mortgage boom and the growth of AI-related borrowing.
The global web of mortgage-backed securities and derivatives was so complex that analysts struggled to understand the risks.

Similarly, data-center borrowing is increasingly difficult to track. Many loans are kept off balance sheets and issued by nonbank lenders like private-equity funds, which have fewer reporting requirements. Chip makers have invested in their customers — a maneuver known as circular financing. Various cross guarantees make it harder to parse who ends up exposed if a loan goes bad.

"We don't understand all the interconnections," said Jeremy Stein, an economist at Harvard University and former Federal Reserve governor who worked in the Obama administration in 2009. While Stein thinks a crisis like 2008 is unlikely, he said he can envision a scenario where the economy takes a bigger hit than after the dot-com bubble. "I would bet that the economic fallout would be greater," he said.

The good news is that hyperscalers like Amazon.com and Microsoft are profitable and have so far mostly paid for data centers with their own cash instead of debt. An AI crash today might cause only $50 billion in losses on data-center loans, a drop in the bucket of the U.S. financial sector, estimates Stijn van Nieuwerburgh, an economist at Columbia Business School.

The bad news is that debt is growing and will likely account for a growing share of spending on data centers. Van Nieuwerburgh projects that if borrowing takes off as expected, a crash in a couple of years might cause $2 trillion in loan losses. And that isn't counting the hit to stock prices. In other words: if you think an AI bust is inevitable, you should hope it happens tomorrow.
The aftermath

Harvard economist Jason Furman calculates that even a 30% drop in stock-market valuations and total stop in data-center construction wouldn't be enough to cause a recession because it hasn't been as big a contributor to GDP growth as is often assumed since so much of what goes into data centers is imported.

His worst-case scenario is something similar to the dot-com downturn. Others see that as the best-case scenario. Van Nieuwerburgh worries about a more severe crisis if the AI boom eventually ends, although he doesn't think that crash is imminent.

Once a crash happens, Washington may no longer be able to blunt the impact the way it has in the past. When unemployment surges, the federal government often turns on the cash spigot to revive the economy. But years of high fiscal deficits have made that harder.
The publicly held federal debt recently crossed 100% of GDP. On the eve of the 2008 financial crisis it stood at just 35%.
Low debt levels going into the crisis made it easier for Washington to borrow its way out by pumping money into the banking sector and keeping public spending high.

This time around, there will be less leeway. Investor worries over the federal debt might also prop up Treasury yields even in a recession, making it much harder for the Federal Reserve to boost growth with low interest rates. Said Stein: "It's not an unreasonable scenario to think about."
